pr.title: Remove a delivered worktree and branch without asking again during cleanup
pr.head: d16b988dd645092e7471b5b6d09859fddeef17d9

summary: The cleanup skill ends an agent session. It checks that the session finished its work, asks the user what to do with anything left, and then releases what the session holds, including the Git worktrees and local branches it created.

Before this change, two Git safety checks made the skill stop and ask the user about worktrees and branches whose work had already merged. Claude Code's ExitWorktree tool compares a worktree with the local copy of the branch it started from, so a stale local main made merged commits look unmerged. git branch -d refuses a squash-merged branch once its remote branch is deleted, because the squash put different commits on main.

The skill already proves delivery itself, in step 4 of "Take stock of the session": every commit is on a remote, or sits at or below the head of the merged pull request. This change makes the release steps rely on that proof. The user's request to clean up counts as consent. Before the skill passes ExitWorktree's discard_changes: true after such a refusal, it runs step 4's checks again, because a subagent may have changed the worktree since. It deletes branches with git branch -D without asking. A change that exists nowhere else is still a gap that the user answers, and the skill discards it only when the user says to.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Gap: work the session owes and has not delivered, such as a commit that exists only in a local worktree. The skill asks the user about each gap.
  • Step 4: the delivery check in "Take stock of the session". It runs git status --porcelain and git log HEAD --not --remotes in each worktree, and for a squash-merged branch it looks up the merged pull request's headRefOid and counts each commit after it as undelivered.
  • Override: a host tool's flag that removes a worktree despite its own safety check, such as ExitWorktree's discard_changes: true.

cards.title: What the review checked
cards.html:
• In a sandbox with a bare remote and a stubbed gh, step 4 reported a gap for a commit after the merged head, an untracked file, a staged change, a detached HEAD with an unpushed commit, and a reused branch name.
  • The first review suggested repeating step 4 before the worktree override, because step 4 runs before the skill stops the session's subagents. This head does that.
  • The review of this head has one open finding: the branch step still deletes with git branch -D on the first step 4's result, so a commit a subagent made after step 4 is lost.

groups.title: Release steps rely on the delivery check
groups.kicker: Worktrees and branches that step 4 cleared go without a second question
intro: The release section removes what the session holds in a fixed order: subscriptions, subagents and background work, reviews, inbox items, worktrees, branches, and stashes. This group changes the worktree and branch steps.

1. Worktrees. The skill removes each worktree that step 4 cleared, without asking. When a host tool refuses because a stale local branch lacks the worktree's commits, the skill runs step 4's checks in the worktree again. It passes the tool's override only when the re-check finds nothing undelivered and the refusal names no uncommitted file, and otherwise asks about the worktree as a gap. It passes an override or --force for a worktree that holds a gap only when the user's answer to that gap says to discard it.
  2. Branches. The skill deletes a cleared branch with git branch -D, because git branch -d refuses a squash-merged branch whose remote branch is gone. It still keeps the branch of an open pull request.
docs/plugins.md describes the same behavior for readers of the plugin documentation.

checks.text: Both steps still apply only to worktrees and branches the session created. The skill's opening section forbids touching the user's checkout or another session's worktree, and this change leaves that rule as it was.

files.note: Release steps 5 (worktrees) and 6 (branches) act on step 4's result without asking. Step 5 runs step 4 again before it passes a host tool's override.

checks.text: On a squash-merged branch whose remote branch is deleted, git branch -d printed not fully merged in a sandbox, and git branch -D deleted it.
In a sandbox, a worktree that was clean at step 4 got an untracked file and then an unpushed commit. Running step 4 again reported each one as a gap, so the override in this step would not pass.

Step 6 deletes with git branch -D on the first step 4's result, which step 5 says is stale once subagents stop. In a sandbox, a commit made after step 4 was deleted with the branch, and no ref kept it. Run step 4's branch check again just before git branch -D.

files.note: Says that cleanup removes a worktree or branch without asking once every commit on it is on a remote or in a merged pull request.
